20488-henry-of-monmouth-volume-1-or-memo:

20489-henry-of-monmouth-volume-2-or-memo:
The second volume of Henry of Monmouth takes up the life of Henry V from his accession. His father, Henry IV, died at Westminster on Monday, March 20, 1413. The new king's proclamation bore date the very next day, March 21.

Never, the biographer writes, was any prince's coming to a throne hailed with more general joy. The volume follows Henry's reign: his claims in France, his campaigns, and the fame that Shakespeare later fixed in the public mind. It closes the two-volume memoir of the most celebrated soldier king of medieval England.
22005-how-to-add-ten-years-to-your-life-:
S. S. Curry ran the Boston School of Expression, and he set out his rules for a longer, fuller life in a book printed in 1915. Its full title promises ten added years and twice the satisfaction. Curry opens with the poet Bryant, who said a simple morning exercise had lengthened his life. The claim sets the tone: small habits, kept daily, change the whole body.

Curry urges readers to wake gladly, breathe deep, stretch, and meet the day without fear. Voice, posture, and cheerfulness all count as health habits in his scheme. The advice is plain and hopeful rather than medical. Modern readers may smile at its faith, but the core counsel, move and breathe and begin early, still sounds familiar.

Business Executives Move for Vietnam Peace organized the wing of the antiwar movement that wore suits. This file holds the program and contents of its first national meeting, held September 27, 1967, at the Statler Hilton Hotel in Washington.

The meeting's remarks included those of its co-chairman, Senator Thruston B. Morton of Kentucky, a Republican breaking with the war policy of the Johnson years. kelly-miller-an-appeal-to-conscience-ame:
Kelly Miller wrote this protest against America's caste code, published by Macmillan in 1920 with an introduction by Albert Bushnell Hart. Miller was dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at Howard University in Washington. Miller argues that the nation judges Black citizens by one standard and white citizens by another, and that this habit shames its claim to democracy. The introduction praises the book's calm temper while summing up that charge.

Five chapters carry the case: Race Contact, Lawlessness, Segregation, Negro Patriotism and Devotion, and Righteousness. Miller attacks lynching and the Jim Crow laws, defends Black loyalty in war, and insists that fair dealing is a moral duty owed to every citizen. The book closes as it opens, as an appeal to the conscience of right-minded America.
monarch-the-big-bear-of-tallac:
Ernest Thompson Seton published this animal biography in 1919, with a hundred drawings of his own. He heard the tale by a fire in the pines of Mount Tallac, in the Sierra Nevada. Two rough hunters told it in broken bits, a sentence at a time. Seton says their gestures and snarls told as much as their words.

Their subject was Monarch, a giant grizzly of the Tallac country. Seton reads the bear's life as a parable of hill-born power. Like the redwood, the avalanche, and the river, such power grows on the peaks and fades on the plains. His nature writing mixes tracking lore with open sympathy for wild animals.
monsieur-de-pourceaugnac:
Molière's farce Monsieur de Pourceaugnac was acted on October 6, 1669. Charles Heron Wall translated it into English prose, with introductions and notes. The introduction calls it nothing but a farce, and one of the best of its kind. Molière himself acted the title part.

A pompous provincial comes to Paris to marry Julia, whose lover Éraste wants her himself. The Neapolitan adventurer Sbrigani organizes the torment. Two physicians and an apothecary attack the visitor with the era's medicine, which Molière mocks savagely. Disguises, false wives, and police officers complete the machinery of this boisterous comedy of vanity.
nasa-tm-19680004505-flight-evaluation-of:
Daniel J. Lesco, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this memorandum in January 1968. Numbered TM X-1488, it gives a flight evaluation of an electrostatic accelerometer. The instrument measures the very low-level accelerations a spacecraft feels in orbit, such as the gentle push of venting gas. Ordinary accelerometers cannot sense such pushes cleanly.

Conventional instruments suffer a null bias, a false output at zero input, as large as the tiny accelerations themselves. The miniature electrostatic design suspends its proof mass electrically, which removes that bias problem. On its first flight test, aboard an orbiting Saturn S-IVB stage on the AS-203 mission, it measured liquid hydrogen venting accelerations at tiny levels. They sat far below a thousandth of Earth's gravity. Lesco compares the readings with other flight measurements and correlates the output with firings of the attitude control system.
nasa-tm-19680018145-synthesis-of-organic:
C. Ponnamperuma and co-authors F. Woeller, J. Flores, M. Ramirez, and W. Allen of Ames Research Center test how organic compounds form under electric discharges in this study. The work simulates the primitive Earth's atmosphere, thought to hold mainly methane, ammonia, and water. Such experiments probe how life's building blocks could arise without life.

Energy sources on the early Earth included sunlight, heat, ionizing radiation, and lightning-like discharges. Discharges act close to the surface, so their products could reach early oceans effectively. The team ran discharge experiments to mimic those prebiotic reactions. Their paper describes attempts to form organic substances by this route. The results bear on chemical evolution before biology began.
nasa-tm-19680024922-optimal-control-of-s:
William P. Kavanaugh, Elwood C. Stewart, and David H. Brocker of Ames Research Center apply random search to satellite attitude control in this 1968 conference paper. Some control problems amount to finding the lowest point of a performance surface. That surface is often unknown, discontinuous, and full of peaks, valleys, and flat regions.

Random search suits such rough surfaces well. The authors review an adaptive random search algorithm from their earlier work. That algorithm had hunted the minimum of a boundary surface from optimal control theory. Here they apply it to satellite attitude acquisition, the task of pointing a satellite correctly. A hybrid computer ran the search described in the paper.
nasa-tm-19710015775-long-term-drift-of-s:
G E Glawe and A J Szaniszlo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 temperature meeting in Washington. It reports how heat sensors called thermocouples drift over very long use. The test pairs used noble and refractory metals with pure alumina insulation. Runs lasted up to ten thousand hours at extreme heat.

Thirty eight pairs aged in air, argon, and vacuum. In air, the best platinum pairs drifted only a few degrees over the full run. In argon, drift grew larger, and thin wires behaved erratically. In one vacuum rig, most noble metal pairs failed within a few thousand hours. The team checked chemical and physical changes behind the drift.
nasa-tm-19720007141-flight-investigation:
Verlon L Head of the Lewis Research Center reported these nozzle flights in January 1972, as NASA TM X-2478. A modified F-106B jet carried engine nacelles under its wings. Three variable flap ejector nozzles were flown in that mounting. Tunnel tests alone cannot show how a wing and fuselage change nozzle behavior. These flights measured the real installed case.

Crews gathered nozzle thrust values during the flights. They also measured boattail drag, the drag on the nacelle's tapered rear. Boundary layer readings near the nozzles completed the data set. Designers could then compare mounted and isolated nozzle performance directly. The work continued a long Lewis program on ejector nozzles for advanced jets.
nasa-tm-19720011982-flight-test-of-carbo:
Thomas E Walton Jr and William G Witte of the Langley Research Center reported this heat shield flight test in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2504. A recoverable spacecraft rode the Pacemaker vehicle system. Its shield was carbon phenolic, half carbon fiber and half phenolic resin. Fiber direction varied across different areas of the shield. The flight pushed heating on the round nose to extreme rates.

The nose suffered the greatest mass loss in the test. High heating rates and likely flaking of char shared the blame. The cone section behind wore down evenly, with uniform char depth. Heating measurements suggested the boundary layer had turned turbulent. Sound sensors in the layer gave a new kind of transition evidence. That sensing idea interested the authors for future free flight studies.
parkman-count-frontenac:

the-chateau-of-prince-polignac:

The telling lingers on the town's strange volcanic ground. Hard rocks rise sheer from a narrow valley, the town clusters round two of them, and a third stands a mile off. The highest, the Rocher de Corneille, once held a castle on its summit. There a great bronze figure of the Virgin, cast from cannon taken at Sebastopol, was to stand. Halfway down stands the cathedral, a gloomy Romanesque pile built out on huge supports, reached by a striking flight of steps. Place itself is the tale's first character.
